title: The Messiah
lead: "Messiah" (Hebrew mashiach, Greek christos) means "anointed one." In the Hebrew Bible the word almost always names a present king or priest; the hope for a future anointed king of David's line grew from the promises to David and the prophets. Christians confess Jesus as that Messiah. Jewish tradition, holding that the messianic age of peace has not come, still awaits him.

sections.b: Israel anointed kings and priests with oil, and "the LORD's anointed" is usually the reigning king: Saul (1 Samuel 24:6), David (2 Samuel 23:1), the king of the royal psalms (Psalm 2:2; 18:50). The high priest is "the anointed priest" (Leviticus 4:3), and Isaiah even calls the Persian king Cyrus God's anointed (Isaiah 45:1). Only Daniel 9:25–26 comes close to using the word as a title for a figure still to come. Most scholars, Jewish and Christian, agree on this. Critical scholars add that a developed hope for an end-time Messiah took shape after the exile, and that the writings of the Second Temple period show many forms of it: a Davidic king (Psalms of Solomon 17), two messiahs "of Aaron and Israel" at Qumran (Rule of the Community 9:11), and a heavenly figure in parts of 1 Enoch.
sections.refs: 1 Samuel 24:6; 2 Samuel 23:1; Psalm 2:2; Psalm 18:50; Leviticus 4:3; Isaiah 45:1; Daniel 9:25–26

sections.h: The hope of an anointed king
sections.b: Early texts that later readers took as pointing to the Messiah include Jacob's blessing of Judah (Genesis 49:10) and Balaam's star and scepter (Numbers 24:17). The promise to David of an everlasting house (2 Samuel 7:12–16) becomes the center of the hope, celebrated in royal psalms (Psalm 2; 72; 110) and expanded by the prophets: a child on David's throne (Isaiah 9:6–7), a shoot from Jesse (Isaiah 11:1–10), a ruler from Bethlehem (Micah 5:2), a righteous Branch (Jeremiah 23:5–6), a humble king on a donkey (Zechariah 9:9).
sections.refs: Genesis 49:10; Numbers 24:17; 2 Samuel 7:12–16; Psalm 2:1–12; Psalm 72:1–20; Psalm 110:1–7; Isaiah 9:6–7; Isaiah 11:1–10; Micah 5:2; Jeremiah 23:5–6; Zechariah 9:9

sections.h: The Jewish view: what the Messiah must do
sections.b: Jewish tradition defines the Messiah by what he accomplishes. Maimonides (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11–12) describes a king from David's line, devoted to the Torah, who leads Israel to keep it, fights the LORD's battles, rebuilds the temple and gathers the exiles; if he does all this, "he is certainly the Messiah." The prophets attach these marks to the messianic age: the exiles brought home, the temple rebuilt, nations beating swords into plowshares, and the earth full of the knowledge of the LORD (Isaiah 2:4; 11:9; Jeremiah 23:5–8; Ezekiel 37:24–28). Since the world is not yet at peace, Jews have long argued that Jesus did not fulfill the role. Nachmanides made this case before the king of Aragon at the Barcelona Disputation (1263). Jewish readers also answer the Christian use of Isaiah 53: Rashi and most medieval commentators read the suffering servant as the people Israel, whom Isaiah elsewhere calls God's servant (Isaiah 41:8; 49:3).
sections.refs: Isaiah 2:2–4; Isaiah 11:9; Jeremiah 23:5–8; Ezekiel 37:24–28; Isaiah 41:8; Isaiah 49:3; Isaiah 52:13–53:12

sections.b: The Talmud (Sukkah 52a) speaks of two messianic figures: Messiah son of Joseph, who will be killed, and Messiah son of David, who will reign. It applies the mourning of Zechariah 12:10–12 ("They will look to me, the one they pierced through") to the slain Messiah son of Joseph. Later midrash and Targum Pseudo-Jonathan (on Exodus 40:11) develop a warrior Messiah from Ephraim, Joseph's son. The idea links the northern tribes of Joseph and the southern tribe of Judah, whose rivalry runs from Genesis 37 to Ezekiel 37:15–28. Christian scholars often discuss it beside the New Testament picture of one Messiah who first suffers and then reigns.

The New Testament proclaims Jesus as Christ, son of David (Matthew 1:1; Romans 1:3–4), and argues from texts it reads as foretelling a Messiah who suffers before he is glorified (Luke 24:26–27). Its key texts are Psalm 110:1, which Jesus himself used to ask how David's son can be David's Lord (Matthew 22:41–46); the suffering servant of Isaiah 52:13–53:12 (Acts 8:32–35); and the "son of man" coming with the clouds (Daniel 7:13–14; Mark 14:61–62). To the Jewish objection that the world is not yet redeemed, Christians answer that the Messiah's reign has begun and will be completed when he returns (Acts 3:20–21; 1 Corinthians 15:24–28).
